fixes.explanation: True, friend. When all the jars were full, she asked her son for another, and he replied, “There are no more jars.” Then the oil stopped flowing (2 Kings 4:6). Her sons kept bringing jars and she kept pouring. The oil lasted as long as the jars did.

Right, baker, he does not tell Gehazi to greet everyone. Elisha, the prophet, tells Gehazi, his servant, “If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not answer him.” No hellos in either direction, so the instruction is to go.
No coins in this house, friend. She says, “Your servant has nothing in the house but a jar of oil.” The word is nothing, except that one jar. Silver coins never come up in the text.

That one's True, baker. The oil didn't quit halfway. She kept pouring until all the jars were full, and she asked her son for another. He replied that there were no more jars, and then the oil stopped flowing (2 Kings 4:6).

Debt is the first blank, friend. Elisha says, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt.” That's the very trouble she cried out about at the start, the creditor coming to take her two children. Now she has what she needs to settle it.
No tithe in this verse, friend. Elisha says, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt.” What she pays is a debt, and then she and her sons live on the remainder.

The neighbors helped by lending the jars, friend, but they're not the answer here. Elisha says, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt. Then you and your sons can live on the remainder.” So the oil pays the debt, and what's left is for her and her sons to live on.

A storehouse is for storing, friend, but that's not what she asks for. She asks for a small room upstairs with a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp (2 Kings 4:10). It's for Elisha, the prophet, so he can stay when he comes to them.

False, friend. Elisha, the prophet, is the one who makes the offer, asking whether he can speak on her behalf to the king or the commander of the army. Her reply is, “I have a home among my own people…” A word with the king is quite an offer, and that's the answer she gives.

Nobody's checking the forecast here, friend. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, says, “Well, she has no son…” and “…her husband is old.” Rain and fields never come up. His answer is all about a son and a husband.

Debt was the other woman's trouble earlier in the chapter, baker, and Gehazi doesn't mention it here. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, says, “Well, she has no son…” and “…her husband is old.” That's what he points out about her. Easy to mix up two women in one chapter.
Yes, baker. She says, “No, my lord,” and then, “Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God.” I bet she's being careful with her heart. The text doesn't say why she answered this way.
His mother, baker. The father says to a servant, “Carry him to his mother.” The boy had cried out, “My head! My head!” before that. I think this is a hard moment, and I'll just say it plain.

The text doesn't record that, baker. She is the one who asks her husband for a servant and a donkey so she can go to the man of God. When he asks why she'd go today, her answer is, “Everything is all right…” That's the whole reply.

That's it, friend. Elisha, the prophet, tells his servant Gehazi, “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” Gehazi came to push her away, and Elisha stopped him. Elisha gives his reason in the same breath: her soul is in deep distress.

Elisha does the opposite, baker. He tells Gehazi, his servant, “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” Gehazi was the one pushing, but Elisha made the call.
Not this time, baker. Elisha, the prophet, says, “…the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” So he says the LORD has not told him what's troubling her.
False is right, friend. Elisha, the prophet, says, “…the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” He says her soul is in deep distress, but that the LORD hasn't told him.
No ring in this one, baker. Elisha, the prophet, tells Gehazi, his servant, “Tie up your garment, take my staff in your hand, and go!” A staff is what he's told to take. Rings stay out of this story.

It's the opposite, friend. Elisha, the prophet, tells Gehazi, his servant, “If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not answer him.” No greeting anyone on this trip. Think of the longest hello you've ever had with a neighbor, and picture skipping all of that.

Riding home first isn't what she says, baker. She tells Elisha, the prophet, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” The text then says, “So he got up and followed her.”

No words from the boy at this moment in the text, friend. It says, “…the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.” Elisha, the prophet, had stretched himself out over him a second time. Sneezes and open eyes are what we're given here.
